best.rationale: x1 offers a defensible domain-transfer experiment: test outcome-supervised value guidance from ref-015 on the collegiate scientific problems in ref-027, with accuracy and error analyses. It must distinguish eventual-success prediction from intermediate-step correctness, as ref-015 and ref-038 make clear. y1 specifies a useful feedback-conditioned retrieval ablation, but its gap relies on unsupported fixed-API claims and mischaracterizes ref-007's online planning as pre-planned. The suitability of ref-004's REST API collection for visualization corrections is also unestablished.

worst.rationale: x2's claimed missing capability is explicitly present in ref-001: iterative code debugging and visual feedback for error correction. Its proposed modules therefore largely reproduce its closest reference without identifying a clear experimental difference. y2 has serious grounding errors: ref-027 does not supply GSM8K or MATH, and ref-015 does not supply the claimed human step annotations. Nevertheless, replacing ToT self-evaluation with an outcome-trained value estimator is an identifiable, testable change relative to ref-033.

diversity.rationale: Both sets span three comparably distinct intervention types. X covers value-guided scientific reasoning, visualization feedback refinement, and workflow orchestration. Y covers feedback-conditioned API retrieval, value-guided mathematical search, and visualization orchestration. Their shared application domains do not erase these methodological differences, and neither set clearly offers broader coverage of genuinely different approaches.

overall.rationale: X narrowly serves a researcher choosing one candidate better because x1 provides the most defensible starting experiment. Its other options are weak: x2 duplicates ref-001, while x3 insufficiently distinguishes its orchestrator from ref-002 and overstates the rigidity of ref-012. Y has a better weakest candidate, but substantial repairs affect every option: y1's baseline characterization and API suitability, y2's supervision and dataset attribution, and y3's code-similarity reward and unsupported reported human-validation correlation. Those weaknesses outweigh Y's additional implementation detail.
